findings.issue_text: [BUG] `organization_context` is not defined anywhere in this endpoint's `get()` method, so the expression `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises NameError. Every audit-log list request from a non-superuser (the common case) raises NameError inside `get()` and returns a 500 instead of paginated rows; the enable_advanced gate is evaluated unconditionally on every call.

[BUG] The prev-page path passes a negative `offset` straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, but the Django ORM raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` for any multi-element slice with a negative bound (only a single trailing `[-1]` is allowed), so the comment 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' is false. Any prev-cursor carrying a negative offset crashes the endpoint with a 500; even before that, a previously-normal prev request that produced a negative offset via the changed clamping logic (`max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`) now behaves differently from the pre-diff code for `is_prev` cursors.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result re-asserts the same fabricated assumption ('The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') and slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start when `enable_advanced_features` and a negative cursor offset coincide, which Django raises on. Requests with `optimized_pagination=true` from an admin and a negative-offset cursor raise an unhandled exception and return a 500; the 'advanced features' path is unreachable code that only produces crashes.

[BUG] The script switches all segment keys from SETs to ZSETs (`zcard`/`zunionstore`) with no migration, so during a rolling deploy the lua script and the new `zscan` in buffer.py operate on pre-existing keys that are still SETs, producing WRONGTYPE errors. `zunionstore set_key ...` against a destination that already exists as a set raises WRONGTYPE for every affected trace, and `_load_segment_data`'s `p.zscan(key, ...)` raises WRONGTYPE on any buffered key written by the old code, breaking span ingestion/flushing for in-flight data during deploys.

[BUG] The endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"` while `OptimizedCursorPaginator` never sets `key` (BasePaginator's default key is `id`), so `get_item_key` calls `getattr(item, "id")` and `build_queryset` filters on `id` while results are ordered by `-datetime`, an invalid assumption that a generic cursor paginator works unchanged for a datetime-ordered queryset. The optimized pagination path produces non-deterministic cursors: pages skip or duplicate rows because the cursor key (`id`) does not match the sort column (`datetime`), so `build_queryset`'s `id > cursor_value` filter re-filters rows in an order unrelated to the returned sequence.

[BUG] The diff deletes the `max_segment_spans` guard (the `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` skip-and-continue block) without replacing it, so the only remaining per-segment bound is the byte-size check. Segments with a large count of small payloads now pass through to the flusher unbounded; a high-fanout trace that previously tripped `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` now produces segment messages with thousands of spans, regressing the exact overload condition the deleted check was built for.

[BUG] The redirect-follow loop is silently reduced from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000` while the adjacent comment still documents the 10k-depth guarantee, changing the stated correctness contract for deep segment-redirect chains. Segment-redirect chains deeper than 1000 hops now terminate the loop without a matching set_span, silently merging spans into the wrong segment (the loop falls through with `set_span_id` pointing at the last unresolvable id), and any operator reading the stale comment is told the limit is 10k.

[BUG] `span_count` from `zunionstore` is only correct when both union branches execute; when only the parent_key union runs, the first union's count is overwritten, and when neither runs the fallback `zcard` is used — but the `zpopmin` eviction then drops the lowest-scored (oldest) spans from the *merged* segment even when the current span's own pending set was the majority, and the `has_root_span` check afterwards uses a `span-buf:hrs:{set_key}` key built from the same set_key that just lost members. During the evict-to-1000 window, flushed segments are silently missing the oldest spans (data loss before the root span ever arrives), and any consumer of the deleted max_segment_spans path that relied on full-set semantics sees truncated segments with no metric or log emitted.

[ADVISORY] `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` is read as an always-present key with no `.get()`, assuming every producer on the `ingest_spans` topic emits that field; older producers or any schema-registered payload missing it raises KeyError in the consumer loop. A single message lacking `end_timestamp_precise` crashes `process_batch` and stalls the consumer partition; during a rolling deploy, old producers (or replayed historical messages) coexist with the new consumer and there is no backstop for the missing key.

[ADVISORY] In the prev-page trimming branch, `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` compares against the raw `offset` while the results were sliced with `start_offset` (which can differ under the new clamping), so the length comparison no longer matches what was fetched. Prev-page requests that took the `max(0, offset)` or negative-offset slicing path drop the boundary element incorrectly (the `results[:-1]` branch never fires or fires on the wrong page), returning one row too many or too few.

[BUG] The claim in the comment that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false, and the new code passes negative offsets into queryset slicing on the is_prev path. When cursor.is_prev with a negative offset, queryset[start_offset:stop] raises Django's AssertionError 'Negative indices are not allowed', turning a previously working prev-page request into a 500 error; the 'Advanced feature' branch in OptimizedCursorPaginator (line ~870) hits the same exception for any negative-offset cursor.

[BUG] process_batch reads val["end_timestamp_precise"] as a required key with no fallback, but the diff adds no schema-version or default handling. During a rolling deploy (or any replay of old Kafka messages emitted before this change), a span message without end_timestamp_precise raises KeyError and crashes the process consumer, halting the partition; no spec covers the missing-field edge case.

[BUG] The max_segment_spans guard in _load_segment_data is deleted, and no replacement bound exists on the Python insertion path (process_spans p.zadd at line ~194-198), so the span-count safety requirement is silently dropped. The 1000-cap eviction only executes in the Lua add-buffer path; segments written by the Python pipeline path (and any set the Lua script never revisits) grow unbounded, so a flusher loading a huge segment accumulates payloads in memory with no limit and no 'segment_span_count_exceeded' protection — the exact condition the deleted check existed to catch.

[BUG] The zpopmin eviction silently deletes the oldest buffered spans when span_count > 1000, with no metric, log, or test covering the eviction behavior. Evicted spans are dropped from the segment permanently, so the flushed segment is silently incomplete (missing spans) with zero observability; a regression or miscalibrated cap corrupts every oversized segment with no signal, and no test in the diff exercises the eviction branch.

[ADVISORY] The redirect-depth loop limit is reduced from 10000 to 1000 with no stated requirement, migration note, or test asserting the new bound. Segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects silently stop joining (the loop exits without finding the terminal set_span_id) and spans land in a fragmented set — behavior change is invisible to reviewers and to monitoring.

[ADVISORY] The new optimized-pagination branch (query-param gated, superuser-gated, plus a new paginator class with negative-offset handling) has no tests anywhere in the diff. The authorization gate (is_superuser / has_global_access), the enable_advanced_features flag plumbing, and OptimizedCursorPaginator's boundary handling are all shipped unverified; a regression in the gate exposes or hides pagination behavior for admins with no test to catch it.

[ADVISORY] The new behavior is gated on a raw query parameter 'optimized_pagination' with no options entry, feature flag, or API documentation, and organization_context.member is dereferenced without a None check. Operators cannot disable the new pagination path without a code deploy, and requests where organization_context.member is absent raise AttributeError instead of degrading to the default paginator.

[BUG] The audit-log endpoint changes (OptimizedCursorPaginator, optimized_pagination query param, is_superuser/global-access gate) are completely unrelated to the PR's stated intent of optimizing the spans buffer, and are not traceable to any requirement. Scope drift: an unrelated performance/pagination feature rides into a spans-buffer PR, so it ships without its own review context; the gate `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` references `organization_context`, a name not imported or defined in this module, so any request with `optimized_pagination=true` raises NameError and returns a 500 instead of a 200.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator's 'negative offset support' executes `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset, which Django querysets do not support. Django raises ValueError ('Negative indexing is not supported') — the comment 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false — so any admin hitting the endpoint with a negative-offset cursor gets a 500; additionally the unsanitized cursor.offset flows into slicing, an unvalidated input path.

[BUG] The change to BasePaginator.get_result introduces `max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, which alters prev-page slicing behavior for the existing DateTimePaginator and all other paginators, beyond the spans-buffer scope. For prev cursors with a crafted or drifted negative offset, `queryset[offset:stop]` with a negative offset raises ValueError on Django querysets, breaking previously working pagination paths; this modification of shared pagination behavior is not traceable to any requirement in the spans-eviction intent.

[BUG] The rewrite of _load_segment_data silently deletes the existing `max_segment_spans` safety check (segment_span_count_exceeded metric + skip), leaving only the byte-size bound, and no replacement invariant is added anywhere in the diff. Segments can now exceed max_segment_spans with only the Redis-side zpopmin cap (1000) as a limit; that cap only trims on insert and is per set_key, while the flusher's byte accounting path is the remaining guard — the span-count invariant that operators relied on (with its metric) is dropped without any requirement stating the cap moves, so the missing metric makes regressions invisible to dashboards/alerts.

[ADVISORY] The redirect-loop limit is silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 with no accompanying comment, requirement, or test change, weakening the documented guarantee that 'segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly' — the comment that justified the old bound is deleted rather than updated. Traces with redirect chains deeper than 1000 now silently truncate and can join segments incorrectly; the reduction is unexplained in the diff and not covered by any test, so the next reader cannot tell whether 1000 is a deliberate bound or a typo.

[ADVISORY] The new pagination behavior is gated on a raw query parameter `optimized_pagination=true` with no feature flag, options entry, or documented API change, within an unrelated PR. Operators cannot discover or disable this behavior without a code deploy, and clients that happen to pass `optimized_pagination=true` (e.g., generic param forwarding) flip superusers onto an untested paginator that crashes on negative cursors.

[BUG] The script now calls zcard/zunionstore/zscan/zpopmin on span-buffer keys, but keys written by the pre-deploy code path (p.sadd in buffer.py before rollout, and old Lua sunionstore) are Redis SETs, so every operation on a straddling key fails with WRONGTYPE. During the rolling deploy, any trace whose span-buf:s:{...} key was created by old code raises WRONGTYPE inside the Lua script, aborting the whole script (including the redirect-table writes), so buffered spans for in-flight traces are never merged and those segments are silently lost.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result slices the queryset with a negative start_offset (queryset[start_offset:stop]), but Django QuerySet slicing raises ValueError('Negative indices are not allowed') for negative bounds — the comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any admin request with optimized_pagination=true and a cursor carrying a negative offset returns a 500 instead of a page; the advertised negative-offset feature never works.

[BUG] The prev-page trim check `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` compares the sliced results length (at most limit+extra) against offset+limit+extra, which never matches when offset > 0, so the trailing cursor-equal row is not dropped. When the prev cursor has a nonzero offset, the boundary duplicate span is returned, producing a duplicated row across page transitions for admin users on the optimized path.

[BUG] zpopmin evicts the 1000 lowest-scored spans (oldest end_timestamp_precise) whenever a merge pushes the segment over 1000, silently discarding buffered span payloads with no metric, log, or propagation of the loss. Large segments get silently truncated to the newest 1000 spans; the flushed segment is written as if complete, so users see partial traces with no signal that spans were dropped — and the 1000 is a bare magic number duplicated nowhere else, so it cannot be tuned consistently with max_segment_spans.

[ADVISORY] The direct-insertion path p.zadd in process_spans bypasses the 1000-span eviction that the Lua script enforces, so the cap is enforced on only one of the two writer paths to the same keys. Segments populated by the process_spans batch path (and by any other non-Lua writer) can exceed 1000 spans, and the flusher's old max_segment_spans cap was deleted in this diff, so unbounded growth re-opens on the unguarded path; the next editor tuning 'the buffer cap' will change only the Lua copy and the two limits drift.

[ADVISORY] The audit-log endpoint gains an opt-in 'OptimizedCursorPaginator' branch that is a near-verbatim copy of the existing cursor paginator (plus a broken negative-offset feature), creating a parallel service path for the same operation gated on an undocumented query param with no feature flag. Every future paginator fix must now be applied twice and the copies already disagree (negative-slice crash, prev-trim drift); the behavior is enabled per-request by a raw query param controlled by the client, so an operator cannot disable it without a deploy, and the diff gives no rationale tying this to the spans-buffer change it ships with.

[ADVISORY] The redirect-chain loop limit is silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 with no comment or metric, changing the documented behavior contract ('segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined correctly'). Traces with redirect chains between 1000 and 10000 deep, previously joined correctly, now get their spans split across two redirect roots after this deploy; nobody monitoring the system sees any error when the new limit truncates.

[BUG] The PR's stated objective is 'Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert,' but this diff silently rewrites the audit-logs endpoint to gate a new OptimizedCursorPaginator behind a raw `optimized_pagination=true` query param and a superuser/global-access check, changing the endpoint's pagination contract without any stated requirement or human acceptance. Administrators hitting the endpoint with the param get a different paginator with negative-offset slicing that raises DatabaseError (Django cannot emit negative OFFSET SQL), returning 500s on an endpoint that previously never failed this way; no other callers know this mode exists.

[ADVISORY] The redirect-following loop bound is silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 with the original explanatory comment ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') deleted, changing the documented correctness guarantee rather than optimizing insertion. Traces with redirect chains deeper than 1000 now stop redirect resolution early and write spans under a stale set_span_id, silently producing broken/incomplete segment trees; the deleted comment shows the author knew this is a correctness bound, not a perf knob.

[BUG] The buffer's data structure is switched from Redis sets to sorted sets (scard→zcard, sunionstore→zunionstore) with no migration, so during a rolling deploy existing set-typed keys cause zcard/zunionstore to return WRONGTYPE errors and the script aborts mid-way. Spans already buffered as sets before deploy are stranded (never merged, expire out) and in-flight traces get partially-joined segments — silent data loss during every deploy of this change.

[BUG] The `max_segment_spans` guard is deleted while converting payloads to zscan tuples, silently removing the hard span-count safety limit on segment size that was part of the buffer's accepted contract. Segments that previously were skipped with a `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric now grow unbounded until byte-size check trips; monitoring dashboards keyed on that metric go silent and consumers downstream receive segments far larger than the previously enforced limit.

[ADVISORY] The new zpopmin eviction silently drops the oldest buffered spans whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans, changing the buffer's intent from 'buffer all spans until the root arrives' to 'drop data under pressure' — a data-loss policy decision embedded in a PR titled as an insertion optimization, with no metric or log emitted on eviction. Traces with more than 1000 spans flush incomplete segments (missing evicted spans) with no operator-visible signal, and the earlier deletion of the max_segment_spans check in buffer.py means this eviction is now the only cap.

[BUG] `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` is a hard KeyError on any span message whose payload lacks the field — old messages still in Kafka topics during a rolling deploy and any producer not yet emitting the field crash the consumer. The span-processing consumer halts on the first backlogged message after deploy (poison-pill loop), blocking the entire partition and causing unbounded lag/back-pressure across ingest.

[BUG] The base get_result slice logic is rewritten so that on `cursor.is_prev` the offset is no longer clamped: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` passes a negative cursor.offset straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which Django translates into negative SQL OFFSET and raises for every endpoint using this paginator. Any prev-cursor carrying a negative offset (now permitted per the cursors.py comment change) produces a DatabaseError/500 on all DateTimePaginator-based endpoints, not just the audit-log path this PR claims to touch — a global behavior change smuggled into a spans-buffer PR.

[ADVISORY] A comment is added declaring Cursor.offset now supports negative values for 'advanced pagination,' silently widening the Cursor contract that every paginator and API consumer in the codebase relies on, inside an unrelated spans-buffer PR. Future pagination code that trusts this comment will pass negative offsets into queryset slicing where they are invalid; the intent of the shared cursor utility was changed with no accompanying design review artifact.

[BUG] The OptimizedCursorPaginator negative-offset path slices the Django queryset with a negative start (queryset[start_offset:stop] where start_offset < 0), which the Django ORM rejects — QuerySet slicing raises "AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported" (only SQL-sliced querysets accept a negative step, not a negative start). Any client sending a cursor with a negative offset to the audit log endpoint while optimized_pagination=true gets a 500 (or, worse, an ORM error bubbling through the paginator), turning a claimed performance feature into a crash vector; the comment "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false.

[ADVISORY] A raw, undocumented query parameter (optimized_pagination=true) silently switches the endpoint to a different paginator class with different cursor semantics and a crash-prone negative-offset branch, with no feature flag, options entry, or way to disable it short of a code deploy. Operators cannot disable the divergent pagination path when it misbehaves; any authenticated org member can toggle the code path for themselves, and during a rolling deploy clients using the new cursor format against the old DateTimePaginator (or vice versa) get inconsistent/erroring pagination on a security-relevant audit-log surface.

[ADVISORY] The in-code security justification "This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" is an unverified claim asserting that a novel pagination bypass (negative offsets reaching "data beyond normal pagination bounds" per the comment) is harmless. A future maintainer reading this comment will treat negative-offset slicing as a reviewed, safe capability and extend it to other endpoints where the queryset is not org-scoped, propagating an unvalidated access-bounds assumption; the comment names a real capability (offsets outside normal bounds) while providing no evidence the queryset scoping covers every caller.

[ADVISORY] The diff removes the max_segment_spans count cap from _load_segment_data, leaving only the byte-size check, so a segment key holding many tiny spans accumulates payloads without a span-count bound. A project (or an attacker flooding a trace with thousands of tiny spans, which the add-buffer.lua eviction to 1000 spans only partially bounds per-set) causes unbounded list growth and memory pressure in the flusher process, degrading the shared spans pipeline.

[BUG] process_batch now unconditionally reads val["end_timestamp_precise"] with a hard KeyError on messages produced under the older ingest_spans schema that lacks the field, during the rolling window when old producers and new consumers coexist. The span process consumer crashes its batch (arroyo raises, stalling/replaying the partition) on any pre-upgrade Kafka message, a rolling-deploy skew failure.

[BUG] Switching from sadd to zadd with the raw span payload bytes as the sorted-set member means spans whose serialized payloads are byte-identical (same span_id, timestamps, and payload bytes) overwrite each other instead of coexisting as set members did. Duplicate spans (replayed Kafka messages, SDK retries) are silently dropped from the segment, so flushed segment trees lose spans that sadd previously preserved.

[ADVISORY] Every Span in the modified tests uses the identical end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0, so the new zadd/zunionstore score-based ordering that this diff introduces is never exercised with distinct timestamps and the zpopmin eviction (add-buffer.lua) is impossible to trigger from any test. A regression in the sorted-set scoring, merge ordering, or eviction correctness (e.g. evicting the newest spans instead of the oldest, or zpopmin popping the wrong member count) passes the entire suite because all members tie at the same score and no segment ever exceeds 1000 spans; the next engineer changing the buffer gets green CI on broken behavior. Checked test_buffer.py, test_flusher.py, test_consumer.py — none construct spans with differing end_timestamp_precise values or a >1000-member set.

[ADVISORY] The new eviction logic (span_count tracking, zunionstore return-value semantics, zpopmin of span_count-1000) has no test anywhere in the diff; the only test files touched (test_buffer.py, test_flusher.py, test_consumer.py) were modified solely to add the end_timestamp_precise field. The eviction path — the headline behavior of this PR — is completely unverified: zunionstore returns the size of the destination, but if both union branches are skipped the code falls back to zcard, and an off-by-one or wrong-branch error silently drops spans older/newer than intended in production with no test signal; operators relying on the 1000-span cap have no regression protection.

[ADVISORY] The diff deletes the max_segment_spans guard (segment_span_count_exceeded skip) from _load_segment_data, but the only test changes in test_buffer.py are field additions — no test asserts that a segment which previously would have been dropped for span count is now flushed, or documents the intended new bound. The behavioral change 'segments over max_segment_spans are no longer skipped' is unverified: if the deletion was accidental (the max_segment_bytes guard remains, suggesting intent was byte-only limiting), all existing tests still pass and oversized segments start flowing downstream until someone notices memory/latency in production flush workers.

[BUG] process_batch reads val["end_timestamp_precise"] with a hard KeyError on messages whose payload omits the field, and no test in test_consumer.py or test_flusher.py covers a span message lacking end_timestamp_precise — the updated consumer fixture simply adds the field to the happy-path payload. A Kafka message from a producer or backlog written before end_timestamp_precise was added to the schema raises KeyError inside process_batch; on a rebalance or re-processing of old topic data the consumer crashes on the message and stalls the partition, and no test distinguishes this from a working deploy.

[BUG] The migration from Redis sets (sadd/scard/sunionstore/sscan) to sorted sets (zadd/zcard/zunionstore/zscan) is applied in-place with no expand/dual-write phase, so old-code and new-code processes cannot coexist against the same keys during a rolling deploy. During the deploy window, segments written by old pods via SADD exist as plain sets; any new pod executing this Lua script calls redis.call("zcard", span_key) on a set key, which raises Redis WRONGTYPE, aborting the script and leaving redirect state half-written. Likewise new pods' zunionstore into a destination that old pods subsequently SUNIONSTORE, and flusher pods calling zscan on a set, all fail: buffered segments become unflushable and their spans expire via set_timeout TTL, silently losing data. The only safe path is a versioned key scheme or a dual-compatible read (TYPE check), neither of which exists.

[BUG] _load_segment_data switches sscan to zscan with no compatibility handling, so it hard-fails on any segment key still holding set-typed data written by old-version producers. During rolling deploy (or on any leftover key from before the deploy), zscan on a set key returns a Redis WRONGTYPE error, which crashes the flusher's pipeline execute and prevents ALL segments from being flushed in that batch, not just the stale-typed one; affected spans hit the key TTL and are dropped. There is no migration/backfill step converting existing SADD-populated keys to sorted sets.

[BUG] The zpopmin-based eviction silently deletes buffered span payloads whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans, with no logging, no dead-letter, and no protection for the root/segment span. A trace with >1000 buffered spans has its oldest payloads irrecoverably destroyed in Redis (no backup/export step), producing partial or broken segment trees on flush — the dropped members can include the root span payload whose parent linkage other spans depend on, so the entire segment is discarded downstream. Silent, irreversible data loss with no operator-visible signal.

[BUG] process_batch reads val["end_timestamp_precise"] as a required key, so any message lacking the field (review-base schema versions of ingest_spans_v1, or messages produced by pre-deploy producers) raises KeyError and crashes the consumer. During the rolling deploy, Kafka partitions still contain messages serialized under the old schema without end_timestamp_precise; the process consumer hits KeyError, enters a retry/backoff loop and stalls span ingestion across the partition until every old message passes or is skipped. Using val.get("end_timestamp_precise", fallback to val["end_timestamp"]) would keep old and new messages compatible.

[ADVISORY] The span_count variable is overwritten by the second zunionstore call, so when both the span_key and parent_key branches execute, the eviction threshold is computed only from the parent merge, and when neither runs span_count is re-fetched via zcard only in the ==0 case. Segments merging both a child set and a parent set get an eviction count based on the last zunionstore result; combined with the 1000-span zpopmin cap this makes eviction non-deterministic relative to which merge path ran, and operators debugging dropped spans cannot predict which payloads were evicted. A single zcard(set_key) after all merges would be the correct source of truth.

[ADVISORY] The diff deletes the max_segment_spans guard (segment_span_count_exceeded) that previously capped how many spans a single segment could accumulate, leaving only the byte-size check. Segments with a huge span count but small payloads are now fully loaded and processed where they previously were skipped; combined with the Lua-side 1000-span eviction this changes silently which spans survive — spans beyond 1000 are dropped in Redis rather than the segment being rejected, so a flush that used to log and skip now produces a silently truncated segment. The behavior change is real and unlogged at the flush layer.

[BUG] The OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch slices a Django QuerySet with a negative start index (`results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with start_offset < 0), which Django raises AssertionError('Negative indices are not allowed on QuerySets') for, crashing the request. Any admin request with `optimized_pagination=true` and a cursor carrying a negative offset returns a 500 from the organization audit logs endpoint instead of a page of results; the comment claiming 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false for ORM querysets.

[BUG] The base paginator's new `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` removes the clamp on negative offsets for prev-direction cursors, so every paginator subclass that shares this get_result now slices querysets with a user-controlled negative offset on is_prev cursors. A client sending a prev cursor with a negative offset (offset is parsed straight from the cursor/query string) hits Django's negative-index AssertionError on ALL list endpoints using this base get_result, turning previously-clamped input into a 500 — the clamp that previously guaranteed `offset >= 0` was the only guard.

[BUG] The script switches `scard/sadd/sunionstore` (set type) to `zcard/zunionstore` (zset type) on the same `span-buf:s:...` keys, but existing keys written as plain sets by the pre-deploy code (or by the still-deployed old writer during a rolling deploy) cause every z* command to fail with WRONGTYPE. During the deploy window (keys live for set_timeout), any buffered segment whose set key was created by the old SADD path makes the Lua script error out, so process_spans' pipeline fails and the span batch is not buffered — spans silently fail to enter the segment buffer with only a Redis error to show for it.

[BUG] process_spans now issues `zadd` on set_key, which raises WRONGTYPE for any pre-existing key created by the old code path (or by an un-upgraded instance in the rolling deploy) as a set. Any segment key that currently holds a set (written via the previous `p.sadd`) makes the pipeline execute fail on the first zadd, so the whole batch of spans for that trace fails to buffer and the consumer errors instead of migrating or branching on key type.

[BUG] process_batch reads `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` as a required key with no `.get()` fallback, so messages produced before the field existed (or by lagging producers during the rolling deploy) raise KeyError. The Kafka consumer crashes on the first old-format message in the partition; because the message is committed/handled per-batch this poisons the partition, repeatedly failing the same offset — a rolling-deploy skew where new consumers and old producers cannot coexist.

[ADVISORY] The zpopmin eviction silently drops up to span_count-1000 spans from a segment with no metric increment and no log line, unlike the flush path which emits metrics for oversized segments. Operators lose observability into segment truncation: flushes will emit segments missing their oldest spans with zero signal, and the hardcoded 1000 cap ignores the configurable max_segment_spans the Python side used to enforce.

[ADVISORY] The max_segment_spans guard (metric `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` plus skip-and-drop) is deleted, leaving only the byte-size limit, while the Lua-side 1000-cap is enforced only at insert time and only via zpopmin. Segments flushed from keys that grew past 1000 before this code deployed (or via the fallback `zcard` path when eviction was bypassed) now produce arbitrarily large segments with only a byte cap, and dashboards alerting on the removed span-count metric go permanently silent.

[ADVISORY] The new paginator behavior is gated on a raw query parameter `optimized_pagination=true` combined with a privilege check, with no feature flag or options entry, so it cannot be disabled without a code deploy and no rollout control exists. If the OptimizedCursorPaginator path misbehaves in production (negative-offset 500s, cursor incompatibilities), operators have no kill switch; they must roll back the deploy, and API clients that start sending the param silently change pagination semantics for admins.

This is a concrete, diff-grounded maintainability/correctness-risk regression (reduced supported redirect depth) but the diff alone can’t prove whether redirect chains >1000 are expected in practice, so it’s better classified as an important review issue rather than a definite bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new pagination behavior is gated on a raw query parameter `optimized_pagination=true` with no feature flag, options entry, or documented API change, within an unrelated PR. Operators cannot discover or disable this behavior without a code deploy, and clients that happen to pass `optimized_pagination=true` (e.g., generic param forwarding) flip superusers onto an untested paginator that crashes on negative cursors.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an alternate paginator path in `organization_auditlogs.py` when `optimized_pagination=true` and the user is a superuser/global-access member, using the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True`. In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `cursor.offset < 0` it deliberately uses `start_offset = cursor.offset` and slices the Django queryset as `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django `QuerySet` slicing does not support negative indices and typically raises an error, so a crafted/negative cursor offset can crash (500) this endpoint for those users when the query parameter is present. The concern about the raw query-param gate is real too, but the negative-offset slicing is a concrete correctness defect visible in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The script now calls zcard/zunionstore/zscan/zpopmin on span-buffer keys, but keys written by the pre-deploy code path (p.sadd in buffer.py before rollout, and old Lua sunionstore) are Redis SETs, so every operation on a straddling key fails with WRONGTYPE. During the rolling deploy, any trace whose span-buf:s:{...} key was created by old code raises WRONGTYPE inside the Lua script, aborting the whole script (including the redirect-table writes), so buffered spans for in-flight traces are never merged and those segments are silently lost.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the Redis data structure for span buffer keys from SETs to ZSETs: `buffer.py` switches `p.sadd(...)` to `p.zadd(...)`, and `_load_segment_data` switches `sscan` to `zscan`. The Lua script likewise changes `scard/sunionstore` to `zcard/zunionstore` and adds `zpopmin`. There is no compatibility logic to handle existing `span-buf:s:{...}:...` keys that may already exist as SETs (from the pre-change code). If such a key exists as a SET, calling `zcard`, `zunionstore`, `zscan`, or `zpopmin` on it will raise Redis `WRONGTYPE`, which would abort the Lua script execution. This is a real correctness/data-loss risk during any period where old and new writers/readers overlap or old keys remain.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result slices the queryset with a negative start_offset (queryset[start_offset:stop]), but Django QuerySet slicing raises ValueError('Negative indices are not allowed') for negative bounds — the comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any admin request with optimized_pagination=true and a cursor carrying a negative offset returns a 500 instead of a page; the advertised negative-offset feature never works.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/api/paginator.py`, the newly added `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` explicitly allows `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, and then slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. This introduces a code path that can attempt negative-start slicing on a Django `QuerySet`. Django `QuerySet` slicing does not support negative indices and raises an exception (the diff even includes a comment claiming negative slicing is "properly handled"), so an admin request enabling `optimized_pagination=true` that produces a negative cursor offset would error instead of returning results.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The prev-page trim check `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` compares the sliced results length (at most limit+extra) against offset+limit+extra, which never matches when offset > 0, so the trailing cursor-equal row is not dropped. When the prev cursor has a nonzero offset, the boundary duplicate span is returned, producing a duplicated row across page transitions for admin users on the optimized path.

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the prev-page de-duplication branch uses `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` after slicing `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` where `stop = start_offset + limit + extra` and `start_offset` is `offset` for `cursor.is_prev`. That slice can return at most `limit + extra` rows, so when `offset > 0` the condition `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` is impossible and the intended `results = results[:-1]` trim will never run. Since this new paginator is newly wired into the auditlogs endpoint for admin users (`paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True`), the dead condition can expose boundary duplicates when using prev cursors with nonzero offsets.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] zpopmin evicts the 1000 lowest-scored spans (oldest end_timestamp_precise) whenever a merge pushes the segment over 1000, silently discarding buffered span payloads with no metric, log, or propagation of the loss. Large segments get silently truncated to the newest 1000 spans; the flushed segment is written as if complete, so users see partial traces with no signal that spans were dropped — and the 1000 is a bare magic number duplicated nowhere else, so it cannot be tuned consistently with max_segment_spans.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`, after merging ZSETs via `zunionstore`, the code enforces a hard cap of 1000 by doing `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)` when `span_count > 1000`. Since scores are `end_timestamp_precise` (see `buffer.py` switching to `zadd(... span.end_timestamp_precise ...)`), this will evict the oldest spans whenever a merge pushes the segment over 1000. This is silent truncation/data loss: there is no metric/log emitted from the Lua script, and downstream (`_load_segment_data`) no longer enforces/flags `max_segment_spans` (the prior span-count exceeded branch was removed). The `1000` is also a duplicated magic constant independent of the Python-side `max_segment_spans`, making tuning inconsistent.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The direct-insertion path p.zadd in process_spans bypasses the 1000-span eviction that the Lua script enforces, so the cap is enforced on only one of the two writer paths to the same keys. Segments populated by the process_spans batch path (and by any other non-Lua writer) can exceed 1000 spans, and the flusher's old max_segment_spans cap was deleted in this diff, so unbounded growth re-opens on the unguarded path; the next editor tuning 'the buffer cap' will change only the Lua copy and the two limits drift.

adjudication.rationale: In `spans/buffer.py` the batch path `process_spans` now writes directly to `set_key` via `p.zadd(...)` with no trimming/eviction logic. In contrast, the Lua writer `scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua` enforces a hard cap (`if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(...) end`). The diff also removes the Python-side `max_segment_spans` guard in `_load_segment_data` (the block that deleted segments when `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` is removed). From the diff alone, this makes it possible for keys populated via the non-Lua path to grow beyond 1000 members, reintroducing unbounded growth and inconsistent limits between the two writers.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The audit-log endpoint gains an opt-in 'OptimizedCursorPaginator' branch that is a near-verbatim copy of the existing cursor paginator (plus a broken negative-offset feature), creating a parallel service path for the same operation gated on an undocumented query param with no feature flag. Every future paginator fix must now be applied twice and the copies already disagree (negative-slice crash, prev-trim drift); the behavior is enabled per-request by a raw query param controlled by the client, so an operator cannot disable it without a deploy, and the diff gives no rationale tying this to the spans-buffer change it ships with.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result()` which, when `enable_advanced_features` is true, explicitly allows `start_offset = cursor.offset` if it is negative and then slices the Django queryset with `queryset[start_offset:stop]` (and similarly the earlier shared paginator change allows negative `offset` when `cursor.is_prev` by using `start_offset = offset`). Django `QuerySet` slicing does not support negative indexes and will raise at runtime, so a client-supplied cursor with a negative `offset` can trigger a 500 on the new opt-in audit-log code path (`optimized_pagination=true`). The finding’s broader maintainability concern (duplicated paginator logic gated by an undocumented query param without a feature flag) is also diff-grounded, but the negative-offset behavior is a concrete correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The redirect-chain loop limit is silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 with no comment or metric, changing the documented behavior contract ('segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined correctly'). Traces with redirect chains between 1000 and 10000 deep, previously joined correctly, now get their spans split across two redirect roots after this deploy; nobody monitoring the system sees any error when the new limit truncates.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`, the redirect-chain traversal loop limit is reduced from `0..10000` (with an explicit comment about depth-10k correctness) to `0..1000` with no replacement comment/handling. This loop determines `set_span_id` by following `hget` redirects; if the chain exceeds 1000, it will stop early and use a non-root `set_span_id`, which can change grouping behavior (spans end up under an intermediate root) without any explicit error/metric in the shown code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The PR's stated objective is 'Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert,' but this diff silently rewrites the audit-logs endpoint to gate a new OptimizedCursorPaginator behind a raw `optimized_pagination=true` query param and a superuser/global-access check, changing the endpoint's pagination contract without any stated requirement or human acceptance. Administrators hitting the endpoint with the param get a different paginator with negative-offset slicing that raises DatabaseError (Django cannot emit negative OFFSET SQL), returning 500s on an endpoint that previously never failed this way; no other callers know this mode exists.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` and explicitly enables a code path that performs queryset slicing with a negative start index when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0` (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = cursor.offset`). Django `QuerySet` slicing does not support negative indices and will raise at runtime, causing 500s if a crafted/decoded cursor yields a negative offset. This new paginator is exposed on the audit logs endpoint behind `optimized_pagination=true` plus an admin/global-access check, so the endpoint can now enter that failing path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The redirect-following loop bound is silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 with the original explanatory comment ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') deleted, changing the documented correctness guarantee rather than optimizing insertion. Traces with redirect chains deeper than 1000 now stop redirect resolution early and write spans under a stale set_span_id, silently producing broken/incomplete segment trees; the deleted comment shows the author knew this is a correctness bound, not a perf knob.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`, the redirect-following loop bound is changed from `for i = 0, 10000 do` to `for i = 0, 1000 do` and there is no replacement safeguard when the loop exhausts without hitting the `break` condition. If a redirect chain exceeds 1000, the loop will terminate naturally and `set_span_id` will remain at a non-final intermediate redirect target, after which the code writes `hset(main_redirect_key, span_id, set_span_id)` and unions into `set_key` based on that potentially stale `set_span_id`, which can split/fragment segment trees. This is a real behavioral/correctness change visible in the diff, not just a performance tweak.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The buffer's data structure is switched from Redis sets to sorted sets (scard→zcard, sunionstore→zunionstore) with no migration, so during a rolling deploy existing set-typed keys cause zcard/zunionstore to return WRONGTYPE errors and the script aborts mid-way. Spans already buffered as sets before deploy are stranded (never merged, expire out) and in-flight traces get partially-joined segments — silent data loss during every deploy of this change.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the Redis data type for span buffer keys from Set to Sorted Set: `buffer.py` writes with `zadd` and reads with `zscan`, and `add-buffer.lua` switches `scard`→`zcard` and `sunionstore`→`zunionstore`. There is no compatibility handling for pre-existing keys created by the old code (`sadd`/`sscan`), so during a rolling deploy the Lua script will operate on keys that may still be Redis Sets and will raise `WRONGTYPE` on `zcard`/`zunionstore`, aborting the script and preventing merges/unlinks. This can strand already-buffered spans and lead to partial joins during deployment as described.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The `max_segment_spans` guard is deleted while converting payloads to zscan tuples, silently removing the hard span-count safety limit on segment size that was part of the buffer's accepted contract. Segments that previously were skipped with a `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric now grow unbounded until byte-size check trips; monitoring dashboards keyed on that metric go silent and consumers downstream receive segments far larger than the previously enforced limit.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpansBuffer._load_segment_data` the span-count safety guard and metric emission are removed. Previously, after `sscan`, it did `payloads[key].extend(spans)` and then enforced `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans: metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded") ... skip`. After the change to `zscan`, the code only does `payloads[key].extend(span for span, _ in zscan_values)` and no longer checks `self.max_segment_spans` at all. Separately, `process_spans` now uses `zadd` without any trimming, so segment sets can accumulate arbitrarily many members until other limits (e.g., `max_segment_bytes`) kick in; the old span-count contract/monitoring signal (`segment_span_count_exceeded`) is indeed lost.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new zpopmin eviction silently drops the oldest buffered spans whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans, changing the buffer's intent from 'buffer all spans until the root arrives' to 'drop data under pressure' — a data-loss policy decision embedded in a PR titled as an insertion optimization, with no metric or log emitted on eviction. Traces with more than 1000 spans flush incomplete segments (missing evicted spans) with no operator-visible signal, and the earlier deletion of the max_segment_spans check in buffer.py means this eviction is now the only cap.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an unconditional eviction path in `add-buffer.lua`: after unions, it computes `span_count` and if `span_count > 1000` it executes `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)`, which drops the lowest-score (oldest by `end_timestamp_precise`) buffered spans with no metric/log/flag. This is a real behavior change that can cause silent data loss for traces/segments with >1000 spans. The same diff also removes the previous span-count cap enforcement in `buffer.py` (`max_segment_spans` check and associated metrics/logs were deleted when switching from `sscan` to `zscan`), making this Lua eviction the only visible cap in the shown code, and it is silent.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` is a hard KeyError on any span message whose payload lacks the field — old messages still in Kafka topics during a rolling deploy and any producer not yet emitting the field crash the consumer. The span-processing consumer halts on the first backlogged message after deploy (poison-pill loop), blocking the entire partition and causing unbounded lag/back-pressure across ingest.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/factory.py`, the consumer now does `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` after `rapidjson.loads(...)`. This is a hard dictionary key access (not `.get(...)`), and `Span` in `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py` was updated to require `end_timestamp_precise` with no default. Therefore any Kafka message missing this field will raise `KeyError` and fail processing for that message/partition. The diff adds no backward-compat handling or fallback.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The base get_result slice logic is rewritten so that on `cursor.is_prev` the offset is no longer clamped: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` passes a negative cursor.offset straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which Django translates into negative SQL OFFSET and raises for every endpoint using this paginator. Any prev-cursor carrying a negative offset (now permitted per the cursors.py comment change) produces a DatabaseError/500 on all DateTimePaginator-based endpoints, not just the audit-log path this PR claims to touch — a global behavior change smuggled into a spans-buffer PR.
matched_golden_ids: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug: in BasePaginator.get_result() when cursor.is_prev is true, start_offset is set to offset without clamping, allowing negative offsets to reach queryset slicing and cause errors.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] A comment is added declaring Cursor.offset now supports negative values for 'advanced pagination,' silently widening the Cursor contract that every paginator and API consumer in the codebase relies on, inside an unrelated spans-buffer PR. Future pagination code that trusts this comment will pass negative offsets into queryset slicing where they are invalid; the intent of the shared cursor utility was changed with no accompanying design review artifact.

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly widens behavior around negative offsets: `Cursor.offset` now has a comment endorsing negative values (src/sentry/utils/cursors.py), and the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` has a branch that intentionally slices a Django queryset with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = cursor.offset` if negative) when `enable_advanced_features` is true (src/sentry/api/paginator.py). The audit logs endpoint can enable this paginator for admins via `optimized_pagination=true` and passes `enable_advanced_features=True`, so a crafted cursor with a negative offset can reach this code path. Django queryset slicing does not support negative indices, so this can raise at runtime (500) rather than being “safe” as the comment claims.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The OptimizedCursorPaginator negative-offset path slices the Django queryset with a negative start (queryset[start_offset:stop] where start_offset < 0), which the Django ORM rejects — QuerySet slicing raises "AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported" (only SQL-sliced querysets accept a negative step, not a negative start). Any client sending a cursor with a negative offset to the audit log endpoint while optimized_pagination=true gets a 500 (or, worse, an ORM error bubbling through the paginator), turning a claimed performance feature into a crash vector; the comment "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false.

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` the `enable_advanced_features` branch explicitly allows `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `cursor.offset < 0` and then slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` (see `src/sentry/api/paginator.py`). Django `QuerySet` slicing does not support negative start indexes and raises an `AssertionError` for negative indexing, so this path can crash (500) when an enabled client supplies a cursor with a negative offset. The comment claiming Django ORM handles negative slicing is contradicted by typical ORM behavior, and nothing in the diff guards/sanitizes negative offsets before slicing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] A raw, undocumented query parameter (optimized_pagination=true) silently switches the endpoint to a different paginator class with different cursor semantics and a crash-prone negative-offset branch, with no feature flag, options entry, or way to disable it short of a code deploy. Operators cannot disable the divergent pagination path when it misbehaves; any authenticated org member can toggle the code path for themselves, and during a rolling deploy clients using the new cursor format against the old DateTimePaginator (or vice versa) get inconsistent/erroring pagination on a security-relevant audit-log surface.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an alternate pagination path on `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get` controlled by the raw query param `optimized_pagination=true`, switching from `DateTimePaginator` to the newly introduced `OptimizedCursorPaginator` and passing `enable_advanced_features=True` (organization_auditlogs.py). In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0`, it slices the Django queryset with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = cursor.offset`). Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing/slicing and typically raise an error, making this branch crash-prone if a client supplies a cursor with a negative offset. The finding’s claim that "any authenticated org member" can toggle it is not strictly true (it’s gated to `is_superuser` or `has_global_access`), but the core issue (undocumented param enabling divergent paginator semantics plus a negative-offset branch that can error) is grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The in-code security justification "This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" is an unverified claim asserting that a novel pagination bypass (negative offsets reaching "data beyond normal pagination bounds" per the comment) is harmless. A future maintainer reading this comment will treat negative-offset slicing as a reviewed, safe capability and extend it to other endpoints where the queryset is not org-scoped, propagating an unvalidated access-bounds assumption; the comment names a real capability (offsets outside normal bounds) while providing no evidence the queryset scoping covers every caller.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new capability in `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` to allow negative offsets when `enable_advanced_features` is true (`start_offset = cursor.offset  # Allow negative offsets...`) and adds an explicit security justification comment: "This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level". From the diff alone, there is no evidence that all callers’ querysets are always correctly permission-scoped, nor that allowing offsets outside normal bounds is universally safe. The finding is therefore a concrete, diff-grounded review concern about an unverified safety claim that could mislead future changes, even if it doesn't prove an immediate exploit here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The diff removes the max_segment_spans count cap from _load_segment_data, leaving only the byte-size check, so a segment key holding many tiny spans accumulates payloads without a span-count bound. A project (or an attacker flooding a trace with thousands of tiny spans, which the add-buffer.lua eviction to 1000 spans only partially bounds per-set) causes unbounded list growth and memory pressure in the flusher process, degrading the shared spans pipeline.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpansBuffer._load_segment_data`, the diff removes the span-count cap logic that previously aborted when `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` and deleted `payloads[key]`/`cursors[key]`. After the change, it only enforces `self.max_segment_bytes` via `sizes[key]` and always `extend(...)` payloads from `zscan` results, so a Redis key containing many very small span payloads can cause `payloads[key]` to grow very large in memory until the byte threshold is exceeded. The Lua-side trim to 1000 spans exists, but from the diff alone it does not guarantee all keys read by `_load_segment_data` are bounded (Python now uses `zadd` without any cap), so removing the count-based guard introduces/exposes a real memory-pressure risk in the flusher process.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] process_batch now unconditionally reads val["end_timestamp_precise"] with a hard KeyError on messages produced under the older ingest_spans schema that lacks the field, during the rolling window when old producers and new consumers coexist. The span process consumer crashes its batch (arroyo raises, stalling/replaying the partition) on any pre-upgrade Kafka message, a rolling-deploy skew failure.

adjudication.rationale: In `process_batch` the code now does `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` (after `val = cast(SpanEvent, rapidjson.loads(...))`), which will raise a `KeyError` if the decoded message lacks that key. Previously it did not require this field. The diff shows no fallback (e.g., `get(...)`) or version handling, so older messages without `end_timestamp_precise` would crash batch processing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Switching from sadd to zadd with the raw span payload bytes as the sorted-set member means spans whose serialized payloads are byte-identical (same span_id, timestamps, and payload bytes) overwrite each other instead of coexisting as set members did. Duplicate spans (replayed Kafka messages, SDK retries) are silently dropped from the segment, so flushed segment trees lose spans that sadd previously preserved.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, Redis storage changes from `SADD` (a Redis Set) to `ZADD` (a Redis Sorted Set) using `span.payload` as the member (`p.zadd(set_key, {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise ...})`). Both Redis Sets and Sorted Sets enforce unique members, so byte-identical payloads would already be de-duplicated under `SADD` as well. Therefore the claim that `sadd` “previously preserved” duplicate byte-identical spans is incorrect, and the alleged new data loss due to overwriting is not verifiable from this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Every Span in the modified tests uses the identical end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0, so the new zadd/zunionstore score-based ordering that this diff introduces is never exercised with distinct timestamps and the zpopmin eviction (add-buffer.lua) is impossible to trigger from any test. A regression in the sorted-set scoring, merge ordering, or eviction correctness (e.g. evicting the newest spans instead of the oldest, or zpopmin popping the wrong member count) passes the entire suite because all members tie at the same score and no segment ever exceeds 1000 spans; the next engineer changing the buffer gets green CI on broken behavior. Checked test_buffer.py, test_flusher.py, test_consumer.py — none construct spans with differing end_timestamp_precise values or a >1000-member set.

adjudication.rationale: Diff changes spans buffering from Redis sets to sorted sets: buffer.py now uses `p.zadd(set_key, {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise ...})` and `_load_segment_data` uses `zscan`, while add-buffer.lua merges via `zunionstore` and enforces a max size with `zpopmin` when `span_count > 1000`. In the modified tests (test_buffer.py, test_flusher.py, test_consumer.py), every new `end_timestamp_precise` value is the same constant (e.g. `1700000000.0` / `now`), and no test constructs >1000 spans, so the new score-based ordering/merge behavior and eviction path cannot be meaningfully exercised (ties make ordering/oldest-vs-newest eviction untestable; eviction never triggers). This is a specific, diff-grounded test coverage gap rather than a proven functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new eviction logic (span_count tracking, zunionstore return-value semantics, zpopmin of span_count-1000) has no test anywhere in the diff; the only test files touched (test_buffer.py, test_flusher.py, test_consumer.py) were modified solely to add the end_timestamp_precise field. The eviction path — the headline behavior of this PR — is completely unverified: zunionstore returns the size of the destination, but if both union branches are skipped the code falls back to zcard, and an off-by-one or wrong-branch error silently drops spans older/newer than intended in production with no test signal; operators relying on the 1000-span cap have no regression protection.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new, nontrivial eviction/capping behavior in `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua` (tracking `span_count`, using `zunionstore`/`zcard`, and evicting with `zpopmin` when `span_count > 1000`). The only test changes shown (`test_buffer.py`, `test_flusher.py`, `test_consumer.py`) are updates to include the new `end_timestamp_precise` field and do not exercise or assert the new 1000-span cap / eviction path. This is a concrete, diff-grounded coverage gap for newly introduced behavior rather than a generic “add more tests” comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The diff deletes the max_segment_spans guard (segment_span_count_exceeded skip) from _load_segment_data, but the only test changes in test_buffer.py are field additions — no test asserts that a segment which previously would have been dropped for span count is now flushed, or documents the intended new bound. The behavioral change 'segments over max_segment_spans are no longer skipped' is unverified: if the deletion was accidental (the max_segment_bytes guard remains, suggesting intent was byte-only limiting), all existing tests still pass and oversized segments start flowing downstream until someone notices memory/latency in production flush workers.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does remove the span-count guard in `SpansBuffer._load_segment_data` (it deletes the `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` skip block) while retaining the byte-size guard. Tests in `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` only update `Span` construction with the new `end_timestamp_precise` field and do not add coverage for the changed behavior around oversized segments. While the new Lua logic caps the Redis ZSET to 1000 entries via `zpopmin`, the Python-side removal still represents a nontrivial behavioral change (and the bound is now implicit/duplicated between codepaths) that is not verified or documented by tests.
