adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The migration from Redis sets (sadd/scard/sunionstore/sscan) to sorted sets (zadd/zcard/zunionstore/zscan) is applied in-place with no expand/dual-write phase, so old-code and new-code processes cannot coexist against the same keys during a rolling deploy. During the deploy window, segments written by old pods via SADD exist as plain sets; any new pod executing this Lua script calls redis.call("zcard", span_key) on a set key, which raises Redis WRONGTYPE, aborting the script and leaving redirect state half-written. Likewise new pods' zunionstore into a destination that old pods subsequently SUNIONSTORE, and flusher pods calling zscan on a set, all fail: buffered segments become unflushable and their spans expire via set_timeout TTL, silently losing data. The only safe path is a versioned key scheme or a dual-compatible read (TYPE check), neither of which exists.

adjudication.rationale: The diff switches existing Redis keys in-place from sets to sorted sets while keeping the same key names (e.g. `span-buf:s:{...}:...`). The Lua script now uses `zcard`/`zunionstore` on `span_key`/`parent_key`, and Python now writes with `zadd` and reads with `zscan` instead of `sadd`/`sscan`. There is no versioned key scheme, dual-write, or type-check/compat logic in the diff. During a rolling deploy, old pods can still create `SET` keys via `SADD`, and new pods calling `ZCARD`/`ZSCAN` on those keys will raise Redis `WRONGTYPE`, breaking the script/flush path and risking data loss via TTL expiry.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] _load_segment_data switches sscan to zscan with no compatibility handling, so it hard-fails on any segment key still holding set-typed data written by old-version producers. During rolling deploy (or on any leftover key from before the deploy), zscan on a set key returns a Redis WRONGTYPE error, which crashes the flusher's pipeline execute and prevents ALL segments from being flushed in that batch, not just the stale-typed one; affected spans hit the key TTL and are dropped. There is no migration/backfill step converting existing SADD-populated keys to sorted sets.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes span segment storage from Redis sets to sorted sets: writes switch from `SADD` to `ZADD` (src/sentry/spans/buffer.py `process_spans`), the Lua script switches `SCARD/SUNIONSTORE` to `ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE` and trims via `ZPOPMIN`, and reads switch from `SSCAN` to `ZSCAN` (src/sentry/spans/buffer.py `_load_segment_data`). There is no compatibility fallback or migration in `_load_segment_data`: it unconditionally pipelines `p.zscan(key, ...)` and then `p.execute()`. If any existing segment key is still a set (from older code), `ZSCAN` on a set key will raise a Redis WRONGTYPE error, causing the whole pipeline execute to fail for that batch. The diff shows no try/except, per-key isolation, or conversion of legacy set keys, so the rolling-deploy/stale-key failure mode described is grounded in the changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The zpopmin-based eviction silently deletes buffered span payloads whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans, with no logging, no dead-letter, and no protection for the root/segment span. A trace with >1000 buffered spans has its oldest payloads irrecoverably destroyed in Redis (no backup/export step), producing partial or broken segment trees on flush — the dropped members can include the root span payload whose parent linkage other spans depend on, so the entire segment is discarded downstream. Silent, irreversible data loss with no operator-visible signal.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`, the new cap logic unconditionally evicts members when `span_count > 1000` via `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)`. This permanently deletes buffered span payloads from Redis with no logging/metrics/dead-lettering in the script. There is also no protection to preserve a root/segment span payload within the zset; eviction is purely based on score order (set from `end_timestamp_precise` in `buffer.py` via `zadd`), so any span—including a root span if it happens to be among the lowest-scored—can be dropped. This is silent, irreversible data loss introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] process_batch reads val["end_timestamp_precise"] as a required key, so any message lacking the field (review-base schema versions of ingest_spans_v1, or messages produced by pre-deploy producers) raises KeyError and crashes the consumer. During the rolling deploy, Kafka partitions still contain messages serialized under the old schema without end_timestamp_precise; the process consumer hits KeyError, enters a retry/backoff loop and stalls span ingestion across the partition until every old message passes or is skipped. Using val.get("end_timestamp_precise", fallback to val["end_timestamp"]) would keep old and new messages compatible.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/factory.py`, `process_batch` now constructs `Span(... end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"], ...)` after `val = rapidjson.loads(...)`. Using `val[...]` makes the field required at runtime; if any consumed Kafka message payload lacks `end_timestamp_precise`, this will raise `KeyError` and can crash/stall the consumer. The diff shows no fallback (e.g., `val.get(...)`) or guard, so backward/partial-schema messages would break.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The span_count variable is overwritten by the second zunionstore call, so when both the span_key and parent_key branches execute, the eviction threshold is computed only from the parent merge, and when neither runs span_count is re-fetched via zcard only in the ==0 case. Segments merging both a child set and a parent set get an eviction count based on the last zunionstore result; combined with the 1000-span zpopmin cap this makes eviction non-deterministic relative to which merge path ran, and operators debugging dropped spans cannot predict which payloads were evicted. A single zcard(set_key) after all merges would be the correct source of truth.

adjudication.rationale: In `add-buffer.lua`, `span_count` being overwritten by the second `zunionstore` does not lose information about the combined merge. The second `zunionstore` unions `set_key` (which already includes the first merge if it ran) with `parent_key`, and Redis `ZUNIONSTORE` returns the cardinality of the destination sorted set after the union. Therefore, when both branches execute, the final `span_count` from the second call reflects the merged result of both unions. When neither branch runs, `span_count` remains 0 and is correctly populated via `zcard(set_key)` before eviction. The claimed non-determinism due to “last merge only” is not supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The diff deletes the max_segment_spans guard (segment_span_count_exceeded) that previously capped how many spans a single segment could accumulate, leaving only the byte-size check. Segments with a huge span count but small payloads are now fully loaded and processed where they previously were skipped; combined with the Lua-side 1000-span eviction this changes silently which spans survive — spans beyond 1000 are dropped in Redis rather than the segment being rejected, so a flush that used to log and skip now produces a silently truncated segment. The behavior change is real and unlogged at the flush layer.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does remove the flush-layer `max_segment_spans` guard in `_load_segment_data` (the `segment_span_count_exceeded` logging + skip block is deleted) and now only enforces the byte-size check while extending payloads from `zscan` results. Separately, the Lua script switches from sets to sorted sets and adds a hard cap: if `span_count > 1000` it `zpopmin`’s `span_count - 1000`, which will truncate data in Redis without any corresponding log/metric at the Python flush layer. This is a real, diff-grounded behavior/observability change (skip+log vs truncation), though the truncation appears intentional rather than an unequivocal defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch slices a Django QuerySet with a negative start index (`results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with start_offset < 0), which Django raises AssertionError('Negative indices are not allowed on QuerySets') for, crashing the request. Any admin request with `optimized_pagination=true` and a cursor carrying a negative offset returns a 500 from the organization audit logs endpoint instead of a page of results; the comment claiming 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false for ORM querysets.

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` (negative) and then does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. For Django ORM QuerySets, negative slicing is not supported and raises an `AssertionError` (the diff’s comment claiming it is handled automatically is incorrect). The org audit logs endpoint can select this paginator for admins (`optimized_pagination=true` + `enable_advanced_features=True`), so a cursor containing a negative offset would crash the request.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The base paginator's new `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` removes the clamp on negative offsets for prev-direction cursors, so every paginator subclass that shares this get_result now slices querysets with a user-controlled negative offset on is_prev cursors. A client sending a prev cursor with a negative offset (offset is parsed straight from the cursor/query string) hits Django's negative-index AssertionError on ALL list endpoints using this base get_result, turning previously-clamped input into a 500 — the clamp that previously guaranteed `offset >= 0` was the only guard.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does not show any prior clamp that guaranteed `offset >= 0`. Before this change, `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` would also have used a negative `offset` (for both prev and non-prev) and would have hit Django's negative-slice assertion if a negative offset were provided. The new code *adds* clamping for the non-prev case (`max(0, offset)`), and leaves the prev case using `offset` (which is effectively the same behavior as before for negative offsets). So the claim that this change "removes the clamp" and newly turns previously-safe input into 500s across all endpoints is not supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The script switches `scard/sadd/sunionstore` (set type) to `zcard/zunionstore` (zset type) on the same `span-buf:s:...` keys, but existing keys written as plain sets by the pre-deploy code (or by the still-deployed old writer during a rolling deploy) cause every z* command to fail with WRONGTYPE. During the deploy window (keys live for set_timeout), any buffered segment whose set key was created by the old SADD path makes the Lua script error out, so process_spans' pipeline fails and the span batch is not buffered — spans silently fail to enter the segment buffer with only a Redis error to show for it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the Redis data type for the same `span-buf:s:{...}:<id>` keys from SETs to ZSETs without any compatibility/upgrade handling. Previously `SpansBuffer.process_spans` wrote with `SADD` (set) and `_load_segment_data` read with `SSCAN`; now it writes with `ZADD` and reads with `ZSCAN` (buffer.py). The Lua script `add-buffer.lua` similarly switches from `SCARD/SUNIONSTORE` to `ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE` on the same `span-buf:s:` keys. During a rolling deploy (or while old keys still exist until `set_timeout` expiry), keys created as SETs by old code will cause `Z*` commands to fail with `WRONGTYPE`, breaking buffering/merging in the Lua script and potentially dropping spans for those segments.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] process_spans now issues `zadd` on set_key, which raises WRONGTYPE for any pre-existing key created by the old code path (or by an un-upgraded instance in the rolling deploy) as a set. Any segment key that currently holds a set (written via the previous `p.sadd`) makes the pipeline execute fail on the first zadd, so the whole batch of spans for that trace fails to buffer and the consumer errors instead of migrating or branching on key type.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the Redis data structure for the same `set_key` from a Set to a Sorted Set: `SpansBuffer.process_spans` used to do `p.sadd(set_key, ...)` but now does `p.zadd(set_key, {payload: end_timestamp_precise, ...})` (src/sentry/spans/buffer.py). Redis will raise `WRONGTYPE` if `ZADD` is executed against an existing key holding a non-zset (e.g., a set created by the prior code). The diff does not add any migration, key renaming, or type-branching to handle existing keys, so pre-existing set-backed segment keys can cause pipeline failures during a rolling deploy or after upgrade.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] process_batch reads `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` as a required key with no `.get()` fallback, so messages produced before the field existed (or by lagging producers during the rolling deploy) raise KeyError. The Kafka consumer crashes on the first old-format message in the partition; because the message is committed/handled per-batch this poisons the partition, repeatedly failing the same offset — a rolling-deploy skew where new consumers and old producers cannot coexist.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/factory.py`, `process_batch` now constructs `Span(... end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"], ...)` after `rapidjson.loads`. This makes `end_timestamp_precise` a required key at runtime (no `.get()` default). adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The zpopmin eviction silently drops up to span_count-1000 spans from a segment with no metric increment and no log line, unlike the flush path which emits metrics for oversized segments. Operators lose observability into segment truncation: flushes will emit segments missing their oldest spans with zero signal, and the hardcoded 1000 cap ignores the configurable max_segment_spans the Python side used to enforce.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`, the new logic enforces a hard cap of 1000 spans per segment by calling `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)` when `span_count > 1000`, which necessarily discards spans (oldest by score) with no logging/metrics. At the same time, `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py` removes the prior oversized-segment handling that emitted `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and `logger.error(...)` and skipped processing when `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`. This diff therefore introduces silent truncation and also replaces the previously configurable `self.max_segment_spans` enforcement with a hardcoded 1000 limit in Lua.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The max_segment_spans guard (metric `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` plus skip-and-drop) is deleted, leaving only the byte-size limit, while the Lua-side 1000-cap is enforced only at insert time and only via zpopmin. Segments flushed from keys that grew past 1000 before this code deployed (or via the fallback `zcard` path when eviction was bypassed) now produce arbitrarily large segments with only a byte cap, and dashboards alerting on the removed span-count metric go permanently silent.

adjudication.rationale: The diff removes the span-count safeguard during segment loading: in `SpansBuffer._load_segment_data` the `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` check and the associated metric/skip-and-drop logic are deleted, and the loader now unconditionally extends `payloads[key]` with all `zscan` results as long as the byte-size limit is not exceeded. While `add-buffer.lua` introduces a 1000-member cap via `zpopmin`, that cap is only applied when that Lua script runs; nothing in the diff guarantees that already-existing oversized Redis keys (from before this change, when sets were unbounded) will be trimmed before `_load_segment_data` flushes them. As a result, flushing can process arbitrarily many spans (bounded only by bytes), and the removed metric will indeed stop firing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new paginator behavior is gated on a raw query parameter `optimized_pagination=true` combined with a privilege check, with no feature flag or options entry, so it cannot be disabled without a code deploy and no rollout control exists. If the OptimizedCursorPaginator path misbehaves in production (negative-offset 500s, cursor incompatibilities), operators have no kill switch; they must roll back the deploy, and API clients that start sending the param silently change pagination semantics for admins.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the optimized path is enabled purely by a raw query param (`request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`) plus a privilege check (`request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`) in `organization_auditlogs.py`, with no feature flag/configuration/option gating. That means rollout/rollback control is limited to code deploys, and admin clients can silently opt into a different paginator (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`, with `enable_advanced_features=True`). This is a concrete operability/rollout concern grounded in the added conditional logic, not a direct correctness defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The gate dereferences `organization_context.member.has_global_access` without a guard; if the request path or a non-member superuser hits this endpoint, `member` (or the attribute) may be absent, raising AttributeError where the previous code never touched member state. Requests that previously succeeded (pure superuser access without an organization member record) now 500 on attribute access before any queryset work runs.

adjudication.rationale: The new code does access `organization_context.member.has_global_access` without an explicit `None` guard, but the finding’s concrete failure scenario (“pure superuser access without an organization member record now 500s”) is not supported by the diff: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` will short-circuit when `is_superuser` is true, so it will not dereference `member` for superusers. Whether a non-superuser can reach this endpoint without `organization_context.member` being present is not verifiable from the diff (permissions/organization_context invariants aren’t shown).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Reducing the redirect-chain cap from 10000 to 1000 changes the documented contract ('segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined correctly') with no comment update, and the mismatch with the has_root_span/flush logic is unobserved. Traces with redirect chains deeper than 1000 now silently produce unjoined/duplicated segments during buffering, with no metric or log distinguishing the truncation; debugging production segment-assembly failures will misattribute the cause.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua` the redirect-chain traversal loop cap is reduced from `0..10000` (with an explicit comment about 10k depth) to `0..1000` and the comment is removed. There is still no post-loop check/metric/log to indicate the chain was truncated; if a redirect chain exceeds 1000, the loop will exit and continue using whatever `set_span_id` it last saw, which can change joining behavior vs. before and fail silently. This is a behavior/correctness regression introduced by the diff, not just a documentation nit.
